exercises.solution:
Comparison table:
| Aspect | General-purpose PRG (Def. 2.1; strong variant Def. 2.15) | Canonical derandomizer (Def. 3.1) |
|---|---|---|
| Stretch | ℓ(k) > k, in practice ℓ(k) = poly(k); any desired polynomial stretch reachable by re-seeding amplification (Construction 2.7) | ℓ(k) as large as possible; target 2^{Ω(k)}; ceiling O(2^k) (super-exponential impossible) |
| Generator vs. distinguisher complexity | G in poly(k); distinguishers may be stronger: uniform PPT (time p(t_G(k)) for every polynomial p), or poly-size circuits in the strong variant | G in poly(2^k·ℓ(k)) — may exceed the circuits it fools: t_G(k) > ℓ(k)², even > 2^k, allowed |
| Uniformity and form of the gap | Uniform PPT distinguisher; gap negligible (< 1/p(k) for every polynomial p) | Non-uniform family {D_k} of circuits of size ℓ(k)²; gap the constant 1/6; 'strong sense' per length |
Why each re-setting fits the application: (i) exponential stretch is needed so that a polynomial number t(n) of coins is fed by O(log n)-bit seeds — otherwise the 2^k enumeration is exponential (Theorem 3.3); (ii) the simulation pays 2^k anyway, so the generator may be exponential-time, and it only faces the emulation circuits C_x of size ≤ t(n)² ≤ ℓ(k)² — smaller than itself; (iii) the guarantee is needed per input x for the specific non-uniform circuits C_x, and since the final procedure enumerates all seeds and majority-votes, only the sign of the mean matters — a constant gap 1/6 (calibrated to error 1/3, since 2/3 − 1/6 = 1/2) suffices, no negligibility required. Closing comparison: Theorem 2.16 runs a polynomial-stretch generator, so feeding t(n) = n^c coins needs seeds of length t(n)^{Ω(1)} = n^{Ω(1)} and enumeration costs 2^{n^{Ω(1)}} = 2^{n^ε} for an appropriate ε (optimizing the stretch gives ∩_ε Dtime(2^{n^ε})); Theorem 3.3's generator has ℓ(k) = 2^{Ω(k)}, so ℓ^{-1}(n^c) = O(log n) and enumeration costs 2^{O(log n)}·poly(n) = poly(n) — the difference between the two theorems is entirely the stretch, i.e., the seed length needed per coin.

Write k = ℓ^{-1}(t(n)) (the smallest k with ℓ(k) ≥ t(n)) and T(n) = poly(2^k·t(n)). (i) ℓ(k) = k+1: k = t(n) − 1 = n^c − 1; T(n) = poly(2^{n^c}) — exponential, no better than brute force; BPtime(n^c) is not placed in polynomial time. (ii) ℓ(k) = k²: k = √t(n) = n^{c/2}; T(n) = poly(2^{n^{c/2}}·n^c) = 2^{O(n^{c/2})} — exponential. (iii) ℓ(k) = 2^{√k}: k = (log₂ t(n))² = c² log₂² n; T(n) = poly(2^{c² log² n}·n^c) = 2^{O(log² n)} = n^{O(log n)} — quasi-polynomial (subexponential, but not polynomial). (iv) ℓ(k) = 2^{k/2}: k = 2 log₂ t(n) = 2c log₂ n; T(n) = poly(2^{2c log₂ n}·n^c) = poly(n^{2c}·n^c) = poly(n) — polynomial time. So only exponential stretch places BPtime(n^c) in Dtime(poly(n)); stretches 2^{o(k)} leave T super-polynomial (in case (iii), T = n^{O(log n)}). Ceiling argument: let D_k(y) = 1 iff y = G(s) for some s ∈ {0,1}^k, implemented by hard-wiring all 2^k outputs: size O(2^k·ℓ(k)). Then Pr[D_k(G(U_k)) = 1] = 1 (every output lies in the range), while Pr[D_k(U_ℓ(k)) = 1] = 2^k·2^{−ℓ(k)} = 2^{k−ℓ(k)}; if ℓ(k) = ω(2^k) then k − ℓ(k) → −∞, so Pr[D_k(U_ℓ(k)) = 1] ≤ 1/16 eventually and the gap exceeds 15/16 > 1/6. Meanwhile size O(2^k·ℓ(k)) < ℓ(k)² once ℓ(k) > C·2^k (the ratio 2^k/ℓ(k) → 0), so D_k is a circuit of size below ℓ(k)² violating Eq. (3.1). Hence ℓ(k) = O(2^k) is necessary, and 2^{Ω(k)} — which the computation of case (iv) shows is exactly what makes enumeration polynomial — is simultaneously the strongest attainable stretch and the weakest that suffices for BPP = P.

(a) Let p = G(U_k) and q = U_ℓ(k). The overlap Σ_z min(p(z), q(z)) ≤ Σ_{z: p(z) > 0} q(z) = 2^{k}·2^{−ℓ(k)} = 2^{k−ℓ(k)}, since p is supported on at most 2^k points. Hence TV(p, q) = 1 − overlap ≥ 1 − 2^{k−ℓ(k)}; for ℓ(k) ≥ k + 1 this is ≥ 1/2, and for exponential stretch ℓ(k) = 2^{Ω(k)} it is 1 − 2^{−(2^{Ω(k)} − k)} ≈ 1 — the distributions are statistically maximally far apart. No contradiction with Definition 3.1: computational indistinguishability is defined with respect to the class of size-ℓ(k)² circuits, and every test witnessing the statistical distance is more expensive — the range-membership test costs 2^k·t_G(k) ≫ ℓ(k)² (cf. the ceiling argument in Theorem 3.3), exceeding the budget. The derandomization is untouched because it never asks that G(U_k) be statistically close to uniform: it only needs Pr[C_x(G(U_k)) = 1] to stay on the correct side of 1/2 for each emulation circuit C_x, which Eq. (3.1) guarantees. (b) The enumerator E has time 2^k·t_G(k) ≥ 2^k·ℓ(k) > ℓ(k)² whenever ℓ(k) < 2^k, and ℓ(k) ≥ 2^k is impossible (range test), so E is not a circuit of size ℓ(k)² and lies outside the quantifier of Eq. (3.1); emulating uniform machines by circuits (size ≈ runtime) places E's power at ≈ 2^k·t_G(k) ≫ ℓ(k)², confirming it is not among the adversaries the definition holds G accountable against. Conversely, a general-purpose PRG is polynomial-time, so a PPT distinguisher given the seed s can compute G(s) and compare it with its input suffix: it would accept the generator output with probability 1 versus 2^{−k} on uniform input — trivially distinguishable; hence Chapter 2 security can never tolerate seed revelation. A canonical derandomizer can, because the circuits it must fool have size ℓ(k)² < t_G(k): handed the seed, they still cannot run G on it, nor try all 2^k seeds. The common cause of both facts is the same asymmetry: pseudorandomness is relative to the observer's resources, and the derandomization regime lets the generator be the more powerful party. (c) Stretch amplification (Section 2.4) proves security by a hybrid reduction that must evaluate the base generator internally to build the intermediate distributions; sound in Chapter 2 because the generator is poly-time and the distinguishers are PPT, the reduction collapses in the canonical regime because simulating a 2^{Ω(k)}-time generator inside the reduction produces an adversary of size ≫ ℓ(k)² — outside the class the analysis may use. Structurally, re-seeding composes a generator with itself and can only compound polynomial stretches into polynomial stretches; the canonical goal ℓ(k) = 2^{Ω(k)} sits at the information-theoretic ceiling 2^{O(k)} and must be reached in a single application of the seed. The failure is a feature: it forces the one-shot design of the next lesson (many overlapping windows into one seed, security from a hard-to-approximate predicate) and explains why that construction needs a new raw material — average-case hardness — rather than the one-way functions of Chapter 2.
